provider_query: Compare the Go language specification section on defer statements with the Rust Reference page on destructors
answer:
Both mechanisms schedule cleanup, but Go `defer` is an explicit function-level stack of calls, while Rust destructors are automatic, scope- and value-based drops.

### Go spec: defer statements
Source: [The Go Programming Language Specification — Defer statements](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Defer_statements) (language version go1.27). Supporting explanation: [Defer, Panic, and Recover](https://go.dev/blog/defer-panic-and-recover).

- A `defer` statement is `defer` plus a function or method call (not parenthesized; built-in calls are restricted as in expression statements).
- Each time it runs, the function value and arguments are evaluated and saved; the call itself is not run yet.
- Saved calls run immediately before the surrounding function returns—on an explicit `return`, when the function body ends, or while the goroutine is panicking—in reverse order of deferral (LIFO).
- On an explicit return, defers run after result parameters are set and before the function returns to its caller, so they can read and assign named results.
- A nil function value panics when the deferred call is invoked, not when the `defer` statement is executed.
- Defers are tied to the function, not to nested blocks.

### Rust Reference: destructors
Source: [The Rust Reference — Destructors](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/destructors.html). Extra detail (not the Reference): [The Rustonomicon — Destructors](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustonomicon/destructors.html).

- When an initialized variable or temporary leaves its drop scope, or when an initialized place is overwritten by assignment, its destructor runs. Uninitialized values are not dropped; after a partial move, only still-initialized fields are dropped.
- For a type `T`, drop is: if `T: Drop`, call `<T as Drop>::drop`, then recursively drop fields. Struct, enum-variant, and tuple fields drop in declaration order; array and owned-slice elements drop first to last; closure captures by move drop in an unspecified order.
- Locals in a scope drop in reverse order of declaration (temporaries in reverse order of creation). Nested scopes unwind from the inside out. Function parameters are in the whole-function scope and drop last.
- `core::ptr::drop_in_place` runs a destructor manually (for example, custom smart pointers).
- Drop is attached to values and scopes (blocks, statements, match arms, temporaries), not to an explicit statement list. At a non-unwinding ABI boundary, either no destructors run or those up to the boundary do.

### Comparison

| | Go `defer` | Rust destructors |
|---|---|---|
| Trigger | Explicit `defer` of a call | Automatic when a value leaves scope or is overwritten |
| Granularity | Whole surrounding function | Drop scopes (blocks, statements, match arms, temporaries) and fields |
| Order | LIFO among deferred calls in that function | Locals/temporaries reverse declaration/creation order; fields mostly declaration order |
| What runs | An arbitrary saved function call | `Drop::drop` plus recursive field drops |
| Arguments | Evaluated at the `defer` statement | No separate call arguments; the value itself is dropped |
| Return values | May modify named results after they are set | Drop does not rewrite return values the way Go defers do |
| Failure path | Runs during panic before the function unwinds further | Runs on unwind; special case at non-unwinding ABI boundaries |
| Manual control | Only by writing `defer` | `drop_in_place`, moves, and `mem::forget` (the last skips drop) |

They overlap as “cleanup on the way out,” and both use a reverse order for stacked cleanups, but Go’s model is a programmer-managed call stack per function, while Rust’s is part of ownership: every initialized value has a destructor whether or not `Drop` is implemented.
